core: STATE: a sovereign political territory with defined borders, a permanent population, a government, and the capacity to enter relations with other states (what everyday English calls a 'country')
NATION: a group of people bound by a shared cultural identity (ancestry, language, religion, history, sense of common destiny), whether or not they possess their own state
NATION-STATE: a state whose borders and a single dominant national identity largely coincide, with the note that few are perfectly homogeneous
MULTINATIONAL / multi-ethnic STATE: a state containing two or more national groups with no single group dominant
STATELESS NATION: a people with a shared cultural identity, often occupying a traditional homeland, who do not have their own sovereign state
supporting: The four classic criteria of statehood (Montevideo Convention Art. 1, treated as customary international law): permanent population, defined territory, government, capacity for relations
The role of recognition and UN membership in practice, alongside the declarative view that a state's existence is independent of recognition (Montevideo Art. 3)
A single dated institutional figure to model attribution: the UN has 193 member states (since South Sudan's admission in 2011)
outOfScope: Boundary types and how borders are drawn (owned by borders)
The full political-geography overview and forms of government (owned by political-geography)
Geopolitics and power relations between states (owned by geopolitics)
Ethnicity as an identity concept in depth (owned by ethnicity)
Taking any position on specific contested sovereignty or territorial disputes

claims.claim: A state is an independent (sovereign) government together with the defined territory it governs; in international-law terms a state possesses a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states.

A nation is a large group of people who share a common cultural identity, such as history, culture, language, religion, ancestry, traditions, or a sense of common destiny; a nation may exist with or without a state of its own.

State and nation are distinct: one nation may extend across several countries, and one country may include many nations, so cultural identity and political sovereignty do not necessarily share the same borders.

A nation-state is a state in which a single national group is demographically, culturally, and politically dominant, so that state borders and national identity largely coincide; genuine nation-states are relatively rare because few states are culturally homogeneous.
A multinational state contains two or more national groups where no single group is demographically, culturally, and politically dominant.

A stateless nation is a large group of people who share a common cultural identity and often occupy a traditional homeland but who do not enjoy political independence in a sovereign state of their own.
The United Nations has 193 member states, a total reached when South Sudan was admitted in 2011.

Under the declarative theory reflected in Montevideo Convention Article 3, the political existence of a state is independent of recognition by other states; in practice, recognition by other states and admission to bodies such as the UN strongly affect a state's ability to act on the world stage.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether recognition by other states is a constitutive requirement for statehood.
positions: Declarative theory (Montevideo Convention Art. 3): a state's political existence is independent of recognition; if the four criteria are met, the entity is a state.

Constitutive view / practical reality: recognition by other states and membership in international organizations (e.g., the UN) heavily shape whether an entity can function as a state internationally.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the four Montevideo criteria as the classic definition, notes the declarative principle, and adds that recognition and UN membership matter in practice, without ruling on any specific contested case.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strictly 'nation-state' should be applied given that almost no state is perfectly homogeneous.
positions: Strict usage: reserve 'nation-state' for states where one national group is overwhelmingly dominant.
Looser usage: treat many ordinary countries loosely as nation-states.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the OER's criterion (one national group demographically, culturally, and politically dominant) and explicitly notes that few states are perfectly homogeneous, so 'nation-state' is a matter of degree.

sourceRecords.title: The Western World: Daily Readings on Geography, 1.07: Political Geography
sourceRecords.provider: Joel Quam and G. Scott Campbell (College of DuPage), Social Sci LibreTexts
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the core definitions: state ('an independent government, and the territory it governs'); nation ('a large group of people who share a common cultural identity'); nation-state (one national group demographically, culturally, and politically dominant; examples given include Armenia, Egypt, Japan, France); multinational state ('two or more national groups, where no single group is dominant'; examples Indonesia, Nigeria, Belgium); stateless nation ('a large group of people who share a common cultural identity, and who occupy their traditional homeland, but who do not enjoy political independence'). Also supports the note that everyday English conflates 'nation' with 'country.' Only facts/definitions used; all prose rewritten.

sourceRecords.title: Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States (1933), Articles 1 and 3
sourceRecords.provider: Signatory states; treaty text via University of Oslo Faculty of Law treaty library
sourceRecords.notes: Primary treaty text, signed 26 December 1933, widely cited as reflecting customary international law on the criteria for statehood. Article 1: a state should possess (a) a permanent population; (b) a defined territory; (c) government; and (d) capacity to enter into relations with the other states. Article 3: the political existence of the state is independent of recognition by other states (declarative theory). Read via the University of Oslo treaty library copy. Minimal factual quotation only.
